events.text: The broth is too salty and the herbs went in too early, and an old woman at the next stall laughs out loud. This is {npc}, who has sold noodles from the same cart for forty years. "Spirit herbs are shy," {he} says, taking your spoon. "You do not boil them. You introduce them to the water."

effects.log: {npc} teaches you for an afternoon and refuses your silver. "Come back when it tastes of something," {he} says.
{npc} hands you a cup of {his} own broth. You stop arguing after one sip.
It is terrible. You are proud of it. {npc} nods as if that was the right answer.

events.text: You burn the first cut of beast meat black. {npc}, an old noodle seller who has been watching from {his} cart, comes over without being asked, scrapes the pan, and shows you how a spirit beast's meat must be rested before it meets the fire. "It was angry when it died," {he} says. "Let it calm down first."

effects.log: You rest the next cut as {npc} says, and it comes off the fire tender. {npc} eats half of it, as payment.
You get it right on the fourth try. {npc} pretends not to have watched all four.

events.text: Steam rises from the clear broth and the kitchen smells of rain on a mountain. You drink it slowly. Every bruise the year gave you remembers, one by one, that it was supposed to heal.

effects.log: You watch the street until the bowl is empty. It is a good year to be alive in.

choices.text: Share a bowl with a neighbour

effects.log: Your neighbour says it is the best broth on the street. Your neighbour may be biased.

events.text: The stew bubbles for a day and a night, and the marrow turns the broth gold. When you finally eat it your arms feel like someone else's, someone who has never once been tired. It will not last past the year. You know that. Tonight it does not matter.

choices.text: Go out and split a whole cord of firewood

effects.log: You split it before the moon is up. The neighbours stop to watch.

choices.text: Sit very still and feel it

effects.log: The strength sits in you like a coal in a brazier. You decide to use it well.

events.text: Spirit fruit melts into rice as red as a lantern, and when you eat the congee your dantian warms the way a house warms when someone you love comes home. It is the gentlest strength you have ever eaten.

effects.log: The warmth settles in rings, like a stone dropped in a still pond.
You write it in a small book. Someone, one day, will be glad you did.

events.text: The Thunder-Tiger Roast crackles as if the beast still had something to say. When you eat it the air around your hands smells of a storm, and a cup you set down too hard cracks clean in two.

choices.text: Laugh and buy a stronger cup

effects.log: The potter sells you a stone cup. You crack that one too, by the end of the month.

choices.text: Spar with a friend while it lasts

effects.log: Your friend asks for a rematch after the year turns. You both know why.

events.text: The Nine-Treasure Soup is the colour of old gold and takes three days. When you lift the lid the whole street goes quiet. You eat it alone, in silence, as the recipe asks, and for a moment the noise in your heart goes quiet too.

effects.log: The quiet lasts the night. Some of it is still there in the morning.

choices.text: Throw the doors open and share the last ladle

effects.log: A beggar child gets the last ladle and stares at you as if you were a god.

events.text: The table is so full the legs creak. Your family eats until nobody can speak, and then, somehow, keeps eating. Late in the night someone starts an old song, badly, and everyone joins in, worse.

effects.log: They will tease you about it for years. It is the best kind of teasing.
You keep the sight of them, all together and full, somewhere safe.

events.text: Three ministers come to your banquet in plain clothes, which fools nobody, and a fourth sends a servant with a jar of wine and an apology. By the third dish the ministers are arguing about whose province grows the best spirit herbs. By the fifth they agree on yours.

effects.log: The court talks about your table for a season. Doors that were shut open a little.

choices.text: Tell them the herbs were from the market

effects.log: They laugh until they cry. One of them says honesty is the rarest dish at court.

events.text: Your sect's elders come to the banquet looking suspicious and leave looking fond. The young disciples carry the leftovers back to the dormitories like treasure, and for a month the training yard smells faintly of roast tiger.

choices.text: Send the last pot to the gatekeepers

effects.log: The gatekeepers, who never get invited to anything, remember it longer than the elders do.
Everyone stands. For one evening the sect is a family.

events.text: Lanterns, wine, the smell of spirit herbs on a charcoal fire, and every person you have cared about this year at one long table. A guest raises a cup to you. Then everyone does.

effects.log: You raise your tea to them, and they drink to you, and the night is very long and very short.
It goes on too long. They cheer anyway, mostly so you will stop.

events.text: A board goes up outside your inn: SPIRIT DISHES, THIS SEASON ONLY. By noon the queue reaches the bridge. A traveller who says she crossed three provinces for your roast eats it standing up, at the door, because there is nowhere to sit.

effects.log: You give her your own stool behind the counter. She leaves a poem on the wall about it.

choices.text: Put up a second board: SOLD OUT

effects.log: The queue groans. Your legend grows.

events.text: The spirit menu is back on your inn's board, and the regulars order before they sit down. The cook you hired watches you season the pot the way a disciple watches a master's sword.

effects.log: It is a little wrong and very nearly right. The cook glows for a week.
You do it slowly enough that it can be learned. Next year, it will be.

events.text: The invitation comes on red paper with a golden ladle stamped in the corner: the Contest of a Hundred Flavours. Pinned beneath it is a second note in a heavy hand. "I hear you cook. I have won this three times. Come and lose to me in person. {npc}, head cook of the Golden Pot."

effects.log: You enter. {npc}, they say, read your note twice and then went very quiet.

choices.text: Enter, and send {npc} a bowl of your broth

effects.log: You enter. The bowl comes back empty, with no note at all, which is the best review a rival ever gave.
You are a cook, not a contestant. {npc} wins again, and tells everyone you were afraid.

events.text: The first round is cooked in the common room of an inn, on borrowed stoves, before a crowd that drinks through the whole thing. Your dish goes to the three judges last. The eldest of them puts down his chopsticks and says, "Again."

effects.log: They move you on to the next round. {npc} watches you all the way to the door.
The crowd roars. They will follow you to the next round, too.

events.text: The provincial hall of cooks is cold marble and silent judges. {npc} cooks at the next stove and does not look at you once. When the judges taste your dish one judge closes both eyes. When they taste {his}, nobody does.

effects.log: {npc} nods back, stiffly. The final will be between the two of you, and everyone in the hall knows it.

choices.text: Say nothing and clean your knives

effects.log: You clean them twice. Your hands want something to do.

events.text: The judges taste your dish, then each other's faces. It is good. It is not good enough. {npc} is kind about it, in the way that is worse than gloating, and buys you a cup of tea afterwards that you did not ask for.

effects.log: It is good tea. {npc} says next time will be different. You say you hope so.

choices.text: Go home and cook all night

effects.log: You cook all night. None of it wins anything. All of it is better.

events.text: The Grand Feast of a Hundred Flavours: a thousand guests, nine judges, and one dish each. When the last judge lays down the ladle the hall is so quiet you hear the lanterns hiss. Then they say your name. {npc} is the first to clap, and the last to stop.

effects.log: {npc} bows back, lower. "Next year," {he} says. It is not a threat. It is a promise between cooks.

choices.text: Lift the Golden Ladle over your head

effects.log: The thousand guests roar. Your name goes into every kitchen in the province.

events.text: At the Grand Feast {npc}'s broth comes out of the pot sour, and {npc} stands staring at it like a parent at a child who has said a terrible word. Yours wins. The hall cheers. You know exactly which pinch of salt did it.

effects.log: You take it. It is heavier than it looks.
You look away. {npc} looks at you for a long time.

events.text: {npc} turns up at your kitchen door with a basket of mountain herbs and a face like a winter sky. "I hate losing," {he} says. "I hate it more than anything. Show me how you rest the meat."

effects.log: You cook side by side until dawn. By the end of it you are arguing like old friends.
{npc} leaves the herbs anyway. "Next year," {he} says, and means it.

events.text: {npc} has opened a second Golden Pot across the street from the market where you buy your meat, and makes a point of waving at you every morning. The noodles are very good. You hate that they are very good.

effects.log: {npc} serves you personally and does not charge you. It is the strangest truce in the province.
You walk the long way round for a year. Your legs get stronger, at least.

events.text: A young cook, {npc}, has been standing outside your kitchen every morning for a week, in the rain, holding a knife wrapped in cloth. "I want to learn the spirit kitchen," {he} says, when you finally open the door. "I will wash pots for ten years if I have to."

effects.log: {npc} washes pots for a month and then, one morning, rests a cut of meat exactly right without being told.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to come back in a year

effects.log: {npc} comes back in a year, to the day, with better knife work.

events.text: The story is in every teahouse by the end of the month: the Golden Ladle won with a pinch of the wrong salt in the rival's pot. Nobody can prove it. Nobody needs to. Your regulars find other kitchens.

effects.log: Silence is an answer too. Everyone hears it.

choices.text: Go to Yeom Jaesu and confess

effects.log: Yeom Jaesu hears you out and says nothing for a long time. "Cook it again, honestly, one day," is all.

events.text: In a market you have never visited, an old noodle seller tastes your broth and freezes. "There was a cook," the seller says, "a long time ago, who won the Golden Ladle and rested the meat just like this. Where did you learn it?"

effects.log: The noodle seller gives you a second bowl for free and does not stop staring.

choices.text: Say you must have dreamed it

effects.log: "Dreams are where the best recipes go to wait," the noodle seller says.
